notes: Son of William Armstrong, solicitor, of Durham City. Read Law. Died on the first day of the Battle of the Somme leading men of the 18th (Service) Battalion, DLI. No known grave. Awarded the Military Cross in 1915 for actions at Ypres.
From Hexham, Northumberland. Read Theology. Killed on the opening day of the Third Battle of Ypres. His tutor described him as 'one of the most promising men of his year'. Mentioned in Despatches.
Of Sunderland. Read Classics. Part-time student who worked as a schoolmaster before the war. Killed during the landings at Cape Helles in the opening days of the Gallipoli campaign. No known grave.
Son of a Durham colliery manager. Read Natural Sciences. Killed in the Battle of Loos on the first day of the British offensive. Had been at the front for only six weeks.

Of Darlington. Read Classics. One of the oldest casualties in the Register, having remained in service since 1914. Killed during the German Spring Offensive (Operation Michael) while covering the retreat of the 5th Army.

Of Newcastle upon Tyne. Read Mathematics. Transferred from the Northumberland Fusiliers to the Royal Flying Corps in 1916. Killed when his BE2c was shot down by anti-aircraft fire during a reconnaissance mission.

Seventh son of a Durham schoolmaster. Read Modern History. Killed during the assault on Flers on the first day that tanks were used in battle. His elder brother William was also killed in the war (not a Durham alumnus).

Of Stockton-on-Tees. Reading Theology at the outbreak of war. Commission granted in September 1914. Killed in the opening phase of the Somme campaign. Buried in Serre Road Cemetery No. 2, Beaumont-Hamel.

Of Bishop Auckland. Medical student who volunteered immediately on the outbreak of war. Served at Gallipoli before transfer to the Western Front. Killed while tending wounded near the Passchendaele Ridge. Mentioned in Despatches twice.
Of South Shields. Read Law. Survived the Somme and Passchendaele. Killed in the final advance during the Hundred Days Offensive. He had been mentioned in Despatches for gallantry at Arras in 1917.

Of Durham City. Read Classics. Most senior officer in the Register. Killed on the opening day of the Battle of Arras, during the assault on the Vimy Ridge. Had been decorated with the Military Cross in 1916.

Of Hartlepool. Reading Mathematics. Killed on the final day of the Battle of the Somme. CWGC record notes he died of wounds received the previous day. His family received news of his death on Christmas Day 1916.

Of Gateshead. Read Natural Sciences. Killed in a trench raid on a quiet sector of the front. His colonel's letter home described him as 'one of the best officers in the battalion, respected and loved by all who served under him'.

Of Middlesbrough. Read Natural Sciences with Engineering. Served in the construction of the Messines mines — the largest underground explosion of the war. Killed during the detonation and subsequent assault on 7 June 1917.

Of Consett. Read Modern History. One of the earliest casualties in the Register. Killed during the First Battle of Ypres when the BEF suffered catastrophic officer losses. His name appears in the university's memorial chapel record of 1 November 1914.

Of Darlington. Read Modern History. Killed on 1 July 1916 — the first day of the Battle of the Somme and the bloodiest day in the history of the British Army. His regiment suffered 568 casualties that day.

Of Morpeth, Northumberland. Reading Natural Sciences. Killed during the German Spring Offensive (Operation Georgette), the second phase of the 1918 offensive. He had survived the earlier Operation Michael attacks in March.

Of Durham City. Read Theology. Ordained deacon in 1913 before accepting a commission. One of several clergymen in the Register. Killed in the disastrous attack on the Hohenzollern Redoubt following the Battle of Loos.

Of Stockton-on-Tees. Read Mathematics. Killed during the Battle of Arras (Second Phase). His section had been moving into a new battery position when they came under direct artillery fire. Buried with two of his men.

Of Leeds (scholarship student). Read Modern Languages. Killed on the first day of the Somme at Beaumont-Hamel, where the Leeds Pals suffered enormous losses. His tutor at Hatfield later published a memoir in his honour.

Of Sunderland. Read Natural Sciences. Transferred to the newly formed Machine Gun Corps in 1916. Killed during the Battle of Langemarck in the Third Ypres campaign. His mother retained his letters; a selection was later deposited in Palace Green Library.

Of Swansea (Welsh scholarship student). Read Classics. Killed in the assault on Mametz Wood, which was captured by the 38th (Welsh) Division at great cost. One of three Welsh students in the Register. Buried in Dantzig Alley British Cemetery.

Of Chester-le-Street. Incomplete degree (Reading Law). Killed on the opening day of the Battle of Amiens — the 'Black Day of the German Army'. He had written home the previous week that he expected the war would be over by Christmas.

Of Gateshead. Read Natural Sciences. Killed in the Battle of Aubers Ridge — an attack that failed almost immediately with heavy losses, largely due to a shortage of artillery shells. Mentioned in several regimental histories.

Of Barnard Castle. Read Theology. Ordained deacon shortly before the war. Served as Regimental Chaplain before accepting a fighting commission at his own request in 1915. Killed during the Battle of Guillemont.

Of Newcastle upon Tyne. Read Natural Sciences. Killed in the subsidiary attacks at Hill 70 during the Battle of Loos. His body was never recovered. A memorial window in Hatfield Hall chapel was dedicated to him and four other Hatfield men lost in 1915.

Of Sunderland. Medical student. Lost when HMS Hampshire sank off the Orkney Islands — the same disaster that killed Lord Kitchener. Had been attached to the ship as naval medical officer for three months.

Of Durham City, son of the registrar of Durham University. Read Modern History. Killed three days after the opening of the Somme, during continued fighting at La Boisselle. Buried in Ovillers Military Cemetery.
Of Berwick-upon-Tweed. Read Mathematics. Killed during the Battle of the Menin Road Ridge. His battery diary for the months preceding his death is held in the Durham County Record Office.

Of Middlesbrough. Read Law. Awarded the Military Cross for actions at Arras in 1917. Killed during the crossing of the Canal du Nord — part of the great Allied advance in the final weeks of the war. Mentioned in Despatches.

Of Gateshead. Read Modern History. Transferred from the Western Front to the Mediterranean Expeditionary Force in summer 1915. Killed on the second day of the Suvla landing — one of the war's most mismanaged operations.
Of Lancaster. Read Theology. Volunteered within days of the declaration of war in August 1914. Commission obtained March 1915. Killed in the assault on Ginchy during the Battle of the Somme.

Of Inverness (scholarship student). Read Modern Languages (French and German). Killed in the disastrous attack at Poelcappelle — one of the muddiest and costliest days of the Third Battle of Ypres. Body not recovered.

Of Durham City. Reading Law. Killed during the German Third Spring Offensive (Operation Blücher-Yorck). Had only arrived in France six weeks earlier. One of the last Durham men to die in a German-initiated attack.

Of Bishop Auckland. Read Classics. Survived the first day of the Somme. Killed three months later during the Battle of Le Transloy Ridges. His commanding officer wrote that he was 'the steadiest officer I have had the honour to command'.
Of Ashington, Northumberland. Read Modern Languages. Killed during the German strategic withdrawal to the Hindenburg Line (Operation Alberich). Buried in Ancre British Cemetery.

Of Winchester. Read Classics. Killed in the disastrous assault on Scimitar Hill — the final British attempt to break out from Suvla. No fewer than 5,300 British troops died in this single action on 21 August 1915.

Of Hartlepool. Read Natural Sciences. Killed in a German coastal bombardment at Nieuport. The Nieuport sector was held largely by Belgian forces; British artillery units were attached to support them.

Of Spennymoor. Read Theology (ordained in absentia, 1916). The longest-serving officer in the Register. Had served continuously from September 1914. Killed during the Hundred Days Offensive two months before the Armistice.

Of South Shields. Reading Natural Sciences. Served in the Royal Naval Division — an unusual choice for a landlocked Durham man. Killed on 13 November 1916, the final day of the Somme, when Beaumont-Hamel was finally captured after having defied assault on 1 July.

Of York. Read Mathematics. Transferred to the RFC in 1917 from the Yorkshire Regiment. Died of wounds received when his SE5a was shot down by Jasta 11 aircraft. He had fourteen confirmed aerial victories at the time of his death.
Of Sunderland. Read Law. Among a small number of Durham men who served in Mesopotamia. Killed during the unsuccessful attempt to relieve the besieged garrison at Kut-al-Amara. No known grave.

Of Durham City. Read Classics. Killed during the Second Battle of Ypres, the first battle in which the German Army used chlorine gas on a large scale. The DLI suffered terrible casualties. He is commemorated on the Menin Gate and on the University College memorial board.

Of London. Read Modern Languages (French and German). Killed on 11 November 1914 — the exact date that would be declared Armistice Day four years later. Died during the last major German assault at Ypres that year.

Of Hartlepool. Read Natural Sciences. One of only two Majors in the Register. Career soldier; had seen service on the Northwest Frontier before the war. Killed during the fighting for Delville Wood, one of the most intense phases of the Somme battle.

Of Cardiff (Welsh scholarship student). Reading Modern Languages. Killed a fortnight after the Battle of Messines during consolidation of the captured ground. He had been in France for only four months.

Of London. Read Modern History. One of the few Durham men to serve in the Guards. Killed during the German counter-attack at Cambrai — the battle in which British forces first used massed tanks, only to lose most of the ground gained.

Of Durham City. Read Law. Killed during the pursuit of the retreating German army in the final month of the war. His commanding officer's report notes he died leading his platoon in street fighting. Buried in Cross Roads Cemetery, Fontaine-au-Bois.

Of Newcastle upon Tyne. Medical student (qualified 1915). Killed during the Battle of Arras while tending the wounded at a regimental aid post. Mentioned in Despatches. His memorial in University College reads: 'He gave his life for his friends'.

Of Durham City. Read Modern History. Killed on the first day of the Battle of the Somme. Son of Professor Alston Wilson of Durham University. The Wilson Prize in Modern History, awarded annually at the university, was established in his memory.
